Cometh
kum'eth
v. (third person singular present of come; rendering Hebrew participles, Greek erchetai)
From Saxon cymþ, the third person singular present of cuman, to come. In the Authorized Version it frequently renders a Greek present used of the future — the prophetic present, in which what is certain is spoken of as already on its way.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Cometh is the older comes, and in Scripture it carries a distinctive weight: the present tense used of what is certainly approaching. “in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh” (Matthew 24:44) does not merely predict the second advent; the present tense puts it already in motion, and the exhortation be ye also ready follows from that. The palm-branch crowd greets the King with the same participle: “Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord” (John 12:13), citing the psalm of the coming one. It is equally the verb of quiet dependence: “Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation” (Psalm 62:1) — salvation described not as a thing achieved but as a thing arriving from outside. And in the parable of the lost sheep, the shepherd's return is the hinge of the joy: “when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours” (Luke 15:6). Whether of Christ's advent, of salvation, or of the shepherd with the sheep on his shoulders, the verb keeps the initiative with the one who comes.

Webster 1828 Definition

The third person singular of the present tense of come; the older form of comes. In Scripture it is often the prophetic present — what is certainly approaching spoken of as already on its way — used of Christ's advent and of the salvation that arrives from God.

expand to see more

COMETH, v. [Sax. cymþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of come; contracted in modern usage to comes.

2. To move toward; to approach; to draw near; opposed to go.

3. To arrive; to happen; to come to pass; as, the day cometh.

4. In the prophetic style the present is used of the future to express certainty; as, the Son of man cometh.

5. In Scripture, from him cometh my salvation, Psa. 62; the Son of man cometh, Matt. 24.

Key Scripture

Matthew 24:44 — "Therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh."

Psalm 62:1 — "To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun, A Psalm of David. Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation."

John 12:13 — "Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord."

Luke 15:6 — "And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost."

Modern Corruption

The return of Christ has been quietly moved out of the church's working expectation — treated as a doctrine held rather than an event awaited, or else sunk under charts and date-setting schemes that Scripture never authorised. The present tense restores the plain expectation.

expand to see more

Two failures crowd out watchfulness. The first is a practical unbelief that keeps the article in the creed and never lets it touch the calendar; the church confesses that Christ shall come to judge, and then plans as though He will not. Peter foretold precisely this — scoffers asking where the promise of His coming is, since all things continue as they were. The remedy is not excitement but the ordinary readiness Christ commands: a servant found doing his duty when his lord returns.

The second failure is the speculative machinery of dispensational premillennialism, a nineteenth-century system (Darby, Scofield) unknown to any Reformation confession, which divides the return into stages, times the church's removal against a calendar of tribulation, and has produced a long line of failed predictions. The dictionary's position is the historic Reformed one: a single, visible, bodily return of Christ, at an hour no man knows, to raise the dead and judge the world. The millennial question remains open within Reformed orthodoxy; the date does not, because Christ said plainly that it is not given us to know it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew commonly uses the participle of bo' (to come) for imminent action; Greek erchomai in the present indicative frequently carries future reference, the futuristic present of certainty.

expand to see more

Hebrew bo' (H935) — to come in, to arrive, to enter; its participle expresses the one who is coming.

Greek erchetai (G2064) — he cometh; the present indicative of erchomai, often used of certain future events.

Greek parousia (G3952) — a presence or arrival; the technical noun for the coming of Christ.

Hebrew yeshu'ah (H3444) — salvation, deliverance; that which comes from God in Psalm 62:1.

Saxon cymþ — the Old English third singular present of cuman, to come.

Usage

"Of the certainty of Christ's return at an unknown hour: in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh (Matthew 24:44)."

"Of salvation as a thing arriving from outside the self: from him cometh my salvation (Psalm 62:1)."

"Of the shepherd's return with the recovered sheep: when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends (Luke 15:6)."
